text:
Heartless Hunter: The Crimson Moth, Book 1
By Kristen Ciccarelli
Published by Wednesday Books
Reviewed by Blair Pike
Rune Winters, a young woman playing a risky game. She dances between two worlds. One, as a witch known as the Crimson Moth who rescues imprisoned witches before they are executed by the new regime. The other, as Rune Winters, the shallow socialite who plays a part in social events to gain intel.
Her reason for becoming a vigilante — she was forced into turning in her own grandmother in order to survive. Now, the problem: A specific witch, whom her grandmother told her to search out, has been captured by the Blood Guard. Meanwhile, Gideon Sharpe has been hunting the Crimson Moth for months, and has his own dark past with witches viewing them all as malevolent beings who only use magic to grow their power.
This Fantasy Romance (Romantasy) is a classic “enemies to lovers” story with exceptional banter, and reveals the backstories of both characters.
For Services Rendered: A Barker & Llewelyn Novel
By Will Thomas
Published by Minotaur Books
Reviewed by Jennifer Theriot
For Services Rendered, by Will Thomas, is the most recent installment of the Barker and Llewelyn series. The title characters are private enquiry agents (and don’t call them detectives!) in Victorian-era London.
They bear a strong resemblance to Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson, including an almost supernaturally astute main character and a loyal sidekick who tells the tales of challenging and intriguing cases.
Barker and Llewelyn, however, tend to be more personally involved — and personally threatened — by the criminals then encounter and have to employ more defensive moves than Holmes ever does.
In this installment, they face down Barker’s longtime enemy Sebastian Nightwine — a truly dastardly villain who threatens the safety of our heroes and their loved ones — while also attempting to rescue Dr. Sun Yat-Sen from kidnappers.
As usual, the novel is an entertaining romp punctuated with witty exchanges, suspenseful moments, and vivid descriptions that transport a reader to a very different world.
Pinball: A Graphic History of the Silver Ball
By Jon Chad
Published by First Second
Reviewed by Thomas Vose
As a longtime fan of pinball (despite being never particularly good at it — I can never get the hang of nudging), this book was a real treat.
Written in graphic novel format with excellent and detailed illustrations, it starts its story much further back than one would expect — with “ball in the hole” games of yore, then charts pinball’s course through table games, to the “pop a ball up and see where it falls” games of the early 20th century, to the invention of the flipper which firmly established pinball as a game of skill.
This last was particularly important, as many locations, had banned it for encouraging kids to gamble — the story also wonderfully describes the 1976 case in which a skilled player proved that called shots were possible in court.
With historic tables, creators, and a “State of the Pinball Union” at the end, this is a great slice of history for everyone.
